title: Naked triple
rule: A unit is a row, column or box. If three cells in one unit have only three different candidates between them, those digits must fill those cells. Their candidate lists need not be identical. Remove those digits from the other cells in that unit.

scenarios.caption: Naked triple: fill r9c4.

steps.explanation:
Look at column 4. r4c4 has {3, 7, 9}; r5c4 has {3, 9}; r6c4 has {7, 9}. These candidate lists are not identical, but together they contain only 3, 7, 9.

These three cells must contain three different digits, because a digit cannot repeat in column 4. They have only these three digits available, so 3, 7, 9 must fill these three cells in some order. No other cell in column 4 can use any of them, even though we do not yet know their exact order.

Remove 9 from r7c4: {4, 6, 9} becomes {4, 6}. Remove 7 from r8c4: {4, 6, 7, 8} becomes {4, 6, 8}. Remove 7 and 9 from r9c4: {7, 8, 9} becomes {8}.

r9c4 changes from {7, 8, 9} to {8}. Only 8 remains, so place 8 in r9c4.

The triple reserves 3, 7, 9 for r4c4, r5c4, r6c4 in column 4; none of those digits can go in the other cells of column 4.

r9c4 changes from {7, 8, 9} to {8}. Only 8 remains, so place 8 in r9c4.

title: X-Wing
rule: Focus on one digit. If its only two positions in each of two rows form the corners of a rectangle, it must occupy one of the two diagonal pairs. Either way, remove that digit from the other cells of those two columns. The same reasoning works with rows and columns swapped.

scenarios.caption: X-Wing: fill r6c5.

steps.explanation:
Focus on 6. In column 3, the only two positions for 6 are r3c3 and r6c3. In column 9, the only two positions for 6 are r3c9 and r6c9. These four cells form a rectangle.

If r3c3 is 6, then r6c9 must be 6, because r3c3 blocks 6 at r3c9 in their shared row 3. That leaves r6c9 as the only position for 6 in column 9. This uses one diagonal pair.

If r6c3 is 6, then r3c9 must be 6, because r6c3 blocks 6 at r6c9 in their shared row 6. That leaves r3c9 as the only position for 6 in column 9. This uses the other diagonal pair.

Either way, each of rows 3 and 6 gets its 6 in the rectangle. Remove 6 from r3c4, r3c8, r6c5: these cells are elsewhere in those rows.

r6c5 changes from {5, 6} to {5}. Only 5 remains, so place 5 in r6c5.

Either diagonal pair puts 6 inside the rectangle in each of rows 3 and 6. The X-Wing therefore removes 6 from r6c5.

r6c5 changes from {5, 6} to {5}. Only 5 remains, so place 5 in r6c5.
